title: Demystifying Agent Skills: Why They Work-Until They Don't

visual_explainer.blocker: Two GPT Image attempts on 2026-08-18 ignored the grounded single-paper brief and rendered unrelated Agent Memory Radar dashboard/status UI with fabricated paper/date/count metadata. Visual QA rejected both. GitHub binary publication is available; the blocker is paper-identity/grounding failure in image generation.

analysis.tldr: The paper turns agent-skill evaluation from an endpoint-success question into a stage-factorized reuse study. Holding source trajectories fixed, standardized skills outperform direct Workflow Memory and primarily act as procedural anchors; retrieval and invocation quality then become separate bottlenecks rather than reliable proxies for downstream utility.
analysis.problem: Skill systems are usually judged by aggregate task success, which confounds representation, outcome annotations, framework transfer, retrieval, invocation, and execution. That makes it unclear whether a skill helps because it contains better knowledge, packages the same experience more usefully, is easier to transfer, or is simply easier to retrieve.
analysis.core_idea: Run controlled matched studies over the same prior trajectories: compare Raw, cleaned Workflow Memory, and standardized SKILL.md representations; remove success/failure hints; transfer artifacts across agent frameworks; and separately measure embedding retrieval, explicit skill selection, actual execution-time skill use, and downstream verifier success. Contrastive trajectory coding then attributes behavior to concrete skill-use mechanisms.

memory_design.write: Distill selected successful/failed execution trajectories into either cleaned Workflow Memory or a standardized SKILL.md under matched source-evidence budgets; the study also removes explicit outcome labels to isolate their contribution.
memory_design.organize: Treat skills as reusable procedural artifacts whose representation is intentionally compared with direct workflow-memory traces built from the same source experience.
memory_design.read: Expose candidate skill pools during execution and separately evaluate embedding ranking, explicit agent selection, actual skill access, and final task success so retrieval quality is not conflated with use quality.
memory_design.update_forget: The paper analyzes construction, transfer, retrieval, and use rather than proposing an online consolidation, forgetting, or long-running skill-evolution policy.

compared_to: Workflow Memory built from the same source trajectories under matched task conditions
skill retrieval/selection metrics treated separately from full-pool downstream execution
analysis.evidence: Across matched comparisons, skills improve over Workflow Memory by 6.06 points. Contrastive trajectory analysis finds procedural anchoring in 65.7% of skill cases versus 4.5% explicit knowledge injection. As candidate pools grow from 5 to 100, actual-use precision falls from 29.6% to 3.3%, yet downstream success is comparatively stable; exact ground-truth skill invocation is neither sufficient nor necessary for success. The taxonomy is built from 8,135 normalized trials and 238 valid coded labels, with 95.8% human/LLM aggregation agreement (Cohen's kappa 0.952).
analysis.why_it_matters: It supplies a stronger causal baseline for procedural memory: the same experience can become more useful when compressed into a standardized action anchor, but retrieval accuracy still does not measure procedural utility. That reinforces the radar's stage decomposition from representation to retrieval to consumer-facing reuse rather than treating 'skill memory' as one component.
limitations: Most evidence comes from terminal/software-oriented benchmarks and a small number of agent-framework/model pairings, so transfer to other domains and long-lived users is not established.
The retrieval study uses independently evaluated embedding, explicit-selection, and execution arms; it diagnoses stages but is not one end-to-end learned retrieval pipeline.
The paper studies fixed constructed skills rather than months-long libraries whose contents, router, and governance co-evolve over time.

Stable downstream success under poor ground-truth retrieval partly reflects usefulness of non-ground-truth related skills, so standard retrieval labels may themselves be an imperfect definition of relevance.
